why: Count subarrays that contain at least k disjoint equal-value pairs. The number of pairs in a window is the sum over values of floor(count/2), and it can only grow as the window grows. That monotonicity is what makes the 'count subarrays with at least k' two-pointer trick work, with a hash map holding the counts.
hints: Pairs must use distinct indices, so a value seen c times contributes c // 2 pairs, not c*(c-1)/2.
If [l..r] has at least k pairs, every larger window [l'..r] with l' <= l does too. So for each right end there is a largest valid left end L, and all starts 0..L work.
Keep a count map and the running pair total. Extend r, then advance l while the window without bucket[l] still has at least k pairs. If the window is valid, add l+1. O(n).
pitfalls: Use floor(count/2), not 'number of equal pairs'. The second example in the original ([2,2,2,2,2,2], k=3) has exactly one valid subarray.
Removing an element lowers the pair count only when its value's count was even.
Only add to the answer when the current window actually reaches k pairs.
statement:
You are given an integer array bucket (called numbers in the original) and a positive integer n (called k there). Count the contiguous subarrays bucket[i..j] that contain at least n pairs of equal values.

Formally, the subarray must contain 2n elements at pairwise distinct indices i1, j1, ..., in, jn (all inside [i, j]) with bucket[i1] = bucket[j1], ..., bucket[in] = bucket[jn]. In other words, a value appearing c times in the subarray gives c // 2 pairs.

Example: bucket = [0, 1, 0, 1, 0], n = 2 gives 3.

  • [0..3] = [0,1,0,1]: one pair of 0s and one pair of 1s, so 2 pairs.
  • [1..4] = [1,0,1,0]: 2 pairs.
  • [0..4] = [0,1,0,1,0]: three 0s give 1 pair and two 1s give 1 pair, so 2 pairs.
  • Every shorter subarray has at most 1 pair.

Another example: [2,2,2,2,2,2] with n = 3 gives 1, because only the whole array has three pairs.
constraints: • Not stated in the source. Assume 1 ≤ bucket.length ≤ 105, 1 ≤ n ≤ 105 and 0 ≤ bucket[i] ≤ 109.
